## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Ingrid wanting to see the missed bookings on her own numbers and Karim wanting a free test number because his phone system can't tell him what he misses are the same ask, the group name says it plainly, and Andreas (already has his numbers, says the price beats the lost bookings) and Hannes (won't pay at any price) rightly stand apart since neither belongs in that group.
whys.g2: There is no junk on this line; even Hannes's flat refusal is a real answer about what it would be worth, and it was not forced into a group.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, buyer and sending, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) comes after I had already set the first step as the paid €3,000 pilot (20-21), so it belongs next to the commitment step, not after it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 carry the same kicker and the same question; screen 22 (Offer a pilot?) asks again what screens 20-21 already settled (pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel).
founder.missing: Screen 13 takes one price, but I sell on two: the €3,000 up-front pilot and the per-hotel monthly licence; nothing asks for the recurring licence separately. screens.instead: What is the one thing most likely to slow down or stop a hotel group buying, and how long does it usually take? (e.g. a data protection review of guest calls, a check that bookings land in the PMS, a trial at one hotel first)

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it makes sense that Keel shows me the list back and the belief it will test about it.
screens.why2: Data protection review, PMS and a trial at one hotel are everyday words in German hotel groups, readable on first pass.
screens.why3: These are the hurdles I hit in every sales conversation with a revenue director, so I can judge the list from my own deals.
screens.why4: 'A trial at one hotel first' is my own paid pilot, the way I sell, not a hurdle, and the real German gate is missing: the works council (Betriebsrat) signing off on AI handling staff calls.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my data protection friction, but 'within about 4 weeks' is Keel's number, not mine; my pilot runs up to 8 weeks and I never gave a review timeline.
screens.instead: Rows: A data protection review of guest calls / Works council sign-off on the AI / A check that bookings land in our PMS; belief: Most hotel group revenue directors would get through a data protection review of guest calls within the 8-week pilot, or not need it.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it makes sense to pick the one step I want timed and put my own number on it.
screens.why2: Data protection review, PMS and a trial at one hotel are all everyday words in my sales calls with German hotel groups, and the time box is clear.
screens.why3: I sit in these sales cycles and have a real sense of how long a DSGVO review of guest calls takes at a hotel group, so 4 weeks is my own estimate, not a guess.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct, but 'a trial at one hotel first' is my own pilot offer rather than an obstacle, and a works council (Betriebsrat) sign-off, a real German blocker for AI on the phone line, is missing.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my words, 'a data protection review of guest calls', and my 4 weeks, and the 'or not need it' escape is fair for groups that already cleared it.
screens.instead: Which step do you want to test? -- A data protection review of guest calls / A works council (Betriebsrat) sign-off / A check that bookings land in our PMS; time box as drawn.

screens.why1: After cost, price, who agrees and what slows a purchase, asking for the first committed step is the natural close of the commercial step, and it is my pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain, and 'costs them time, data, money or a signature' tells me exactly what kind of step counts.
screens.why3: The first step I ask of a hotel group is my own sales motion, the €3,000 money-back pilot at one location, so I answer from what I do every week.
screens.why4: There is a free-text box plus the 'Leave this out of the study' escape, which fits since a founder might not want to test commitment.
screens.why5: The belief keeps €3,000, money-back and one hotel, but 'now' and 'in most cases' are Keel's additions, and it drops that the fee is credited on roll-out and that the pilot runs up to 8 weeks, which is what makes my offer low-risk to a revenue director.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take? -> belief: In most cases the hotel group revenue director would pay €3,000 up front for a pilot of up to 8 weeks at one hotel, money back if it doesn't pay off, credited on roll-out.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step, Keel shows me how strangers will hear it and what it will test, which is the obvious place for this check.
screens.why2: "€3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel" is exactly how I pitch it to a group's revenue director; nothing here needs a second read.
screens.why3: It is my own pilot offer from the partnership terms, and I know it from every sales call I run.
screens.why4: The step names the action, the amount, the guarantee and the scope (one hotel) in my words, and the bar of no more than 1 in 3 saying probably not or no is a fair test of it.
screens.why5: It still means what I typed, the paid money-back pilot at one location, and dropping "credited on roll-out" is acceptable within nine words.

screens.why1: Right after I set my first real step, and before strangers see the study, it makes sense to ask whether to offer the pilot to those who say yes.
screens.why2: Pilot is my own word, it is in my partnership terms and launch post, and the two chips read at a glance.
screens.why3: Whether I want a pilot list from this study is entirely my call and I know the answer.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, and the two options are distinct and plain.
screens.why5: The hint's line, 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email', drops the step I just typed (pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel), so the yes I would collect is softer than my real ask.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel? Leave your email." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my reservation agents the questions is an obvious last step before the link goes out, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: Two voices, a play button and a flat 400-credit price are plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: I know how the agents on a Munich desk or in a central office talk to guests, so I can judge from a 5-second clip which voice they would answer.
screens.why4: My agents are in Germany, and neither option says whether Daphne or Saskia asks in German, so the choice I actually care about, a German-speaking voice, is not visible.
screens.why5: It says reservation agents as I typed it, and nothing of Codyco leaks into the choice of voice.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German? Daphne (German) ▶ Hear · 5 s / Saskia (German) ▶ Hear · 5 s

screens.why1: Choosing how the revenue directors answer belongs right before sending, and it follows naturally from picking who asks the agents' questions.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'Daphne' with 'Hear her' and 'Still recording' is a product name I have to read twice to understand; a director calls is plainer.
screens.why3: I know my directors are busy people on phones and email, so I can judge whether they would rather tap than talk to a video.
screens.why4: AI video, read and tap, or let them choose covers the real choices, the three are distinct, and the readiness notes help.
screens.why5: The previous screen asked about reservation agents and this one says 'directors' without saying it means the hotel group revenue directors, so the link between the two drifts a little.
screens.instead: How should the hotel group revenue directors answer? AI interviewer on video (ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose

screens.why1: Once the study is set up and the directors' answer mode is chosen, deciding who gets the link is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: Three plain choices in plain words; as a founder I know a named list, a search list, and an open link to post in a group.
screens.why3: I know who I would send this to: the hotel groups I already work with and the directors I can reach by name.
screens.why4: The options are distinct and cover the real ways to send, but 'People I found with Keel' leans on a Contacts page I have not seen in this flow, so its meaning only comes clear from the subtext.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is changed or leaked; this is a sending screen, and my pick 'People I know by name' is kept.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits under the title with the deciding number beside it (Purchase friction: 4 of 8 expect longer than 4 weeks), and the card list agrees with the bar of no more than 2 of 8.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits, but Existing sacrifice counts 7 of 8 without saying why, and the Price card folds two bars into one line, so both need a second look.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry my lines word for word, and the 5% of calls and the €3,000 then €1,000 per hotel are my numbers in my words.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do. The only statement says who the money questions went to, not that I should bring a data-protection pack (DPA, call-recording terms) to the pilot offer or plan for a 1 to 3 month close.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 is visible on every card, the two passes are called 'at the bar' rather than strong, and Ability to pay is held back as too few to call.
screens.instead: Did not hold on purchase friction: 4 of 8 directors expect the data-protection review of guest calls to take 4 weeks to 3 months, so put a ready GDPR/DPA package in the €3,000 pilot offer and plan for a longer close; the pilot itself holds at the bar, 6 of 8, while the €1,000 licence splits 4 to 4.

screens.why_b1: The status 'People disagree' sits right above '4 of 7 lose 5% or more · bar 5 of 7 · 1 short', so I can see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The unit, the 0–15 axis and the 4-for/3-against strip are plain, but two different fives sit side by side (my 5% marker and the '5 of 7' bar), so I had to look twice to tell the people bar from the percent line.
screens.why_b3: The 5% of calls lost after hours, at peak and on holidays is my claim, but 'Existing sacrifice' is Keel's word, not mine, and I never said 'per hotel a month'.
screens.why_b4: '1 short of the bar' plus a pointer to the Price card is generic, and it never says which groups are short (the ones whose call center already covers after hours, the 2% and 4% answers) or that I should aim at groups without that cover.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (8 answered, 7 counted, Karim excluded and why, Hannes counted as 0) and it says outright that a small group is a lean, not a call, so nothing is overstated beyond these answers.
screens.instead: Missed calls: 4 of 7 directors lose 5% or more (6–10%); the three below either already have a call center covering after hours or lost none. Small group, a lean: pitch first to groups without after-hours cover.

screens.why_b1: The 4 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, 2 short, sits right under the verdict, but the status word is 'People disagree', not 'did not hold', so I have to do the sum myself to see that my price missed its bar.
screens.why_b2: The up-front chart is plain (8 people, my €3,000 at a band's low edge, bar at 6), but the monthly chart only adds up to 7 because Hannes's 'would not pay' drops out, and its second strip shows 4 for and 3 against under a header that says 4 and 4, so I had to look twice.
screens.why_b3: Price, with €3,000 up front and then €1,000 per hotel a month, is exactly the pilot fee and licence floor I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only sends me to the Insights tab; it never says that the three lowest answers (Keller at 4%, Lindholm with a call center, Benali with no data) all want proof on their own numbers first, which points straight at a free or measured pilot.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the screen calls it 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and it claims nothing beyond the 4 for and 4 against.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 8 would pay €3,000 then €1,000 a month, the bar was 6, so 2 short. Hannes wouldn't pay at all. The three others below your price all want to see their own missed calls first, so consider a measured trial before the fee.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 of 8 at my price with 5 needed, so I know why there is no call yet.
screens.why_b2: Budget source over the 4 at my price and the bar at 3 of 4 are plain, but the ghost fifth cell needs a second look, and nothing says outright that 3 for already meets the bar.
screens.why_b3: It is built from my €3,000 pilot and €1,000 licence, but 'could find the money for it' is Keel's framing of a belief I never typed as such.
screens.why_b4: 'Waits until 5 have' tells me I need one more director at my price, but not that the lean is my way, or what an existing budget line at 3 of 4 means for selling the pilot.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than the four who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 who would pay €3,000 already have a budget line for it, which leans your way; one more director at your price settles it.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits beside 6 of 8 against a bar of 6 of 8, at the bar, so I know my belief held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who signs off across 8 revenue directors: 4 need the owner and 2 sign alone, both for me, and 2 against, with the bar marker plainly at 6.
screens.why_b3: The card carries my belief word for word: the revenue director decides and the hotel's owner has to agree.
screens.why_b4: Plan for the owner in most deals, with 2 of 8 able to sign alone, tells me to build the owner's sign-off into the €3,000 pilot pitch.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 stays visible, the screen calls it a lean, not a call, and a result exactly at the bar is not dressed up as strong.
screens.instead: Plan for the hotel's owner in most deals and bring them the pilot's money-back terms; 2 of 8 could sign alone, and 2 need a wider group or someone else, so ask early who that is.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "4 of 8 expect longer than 4 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 8", so I see both the verdict and the miss that decides it.
screens.why_b2: I can see what is counted (review length) over 8 people, but the bar shows as "no more than 2 of 8" in the verdict and as "6 of 8" on the strip, so I had to reconcile them; the bar line "You said a data protection review of guest calls" also gives no duration.
screens.why_b3: Purchase friction and "within about 4 weeks, or not need it" are the belief I checked, word for word.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for a cycle of 4 weeks to 3 months" plus the pointer to Insights for what takes the time is concrete enough to plan the pilot timeline around a DPA review.
screens.why_b5: All four against answers fall in a band that starts at my own 4 weeks, so some may be only just over "about 4 weeks"; telling me to plan for up to 3 months softly overstates this, though n=8 and "a lean, not a call" are shown.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 8 directors expect the guest-call data protection review to run past 4 weeks (bar: at most 2), all in the 4-week-to-3-month band, so start the DPA paperwork before the pilot fee is asked and budget 1-3 months; 2 say no review is needed.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar", so I know my pilot belief held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the three answers to the €3,000 pilot question over 8 directors, 6 yes and 2 against, and the bar is marked at 6 of 8, all plain at once.
screens.why_b3: Card title and belief line are word for word what I checked: the revenue director paying €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel now.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" is a concrete next step for my launch: get those six directors onto the paid one-location pilot.
screens.why_b5: n=8 stays visible, the result is said to be exactly at the bar, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" keeps a borderline 6 of 8 from being sold as strong.
screens.instead: 6 of 8 say they would pay €3,000 for the pilot, just at your bar. Book those six into it, but start the data protection review of guest calls now: half of them expect it to take longer than 4 weeks.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (People disagree, Did not hold, Holding up) with the deciding count and bar right beside it: 4 of 8 against a bar of 6, 4 of 8 against no more than 2, 6 of 8 at the bar.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, word for word, down to the €3,000 money-back pilot and the 4-week data protection review.
screens.why_b4: The price quotes point me to a concrete move (prove the missed bookings on the group's own phone numbers, maybe a free test number, before asking for €3,000), but the screen never says it, and Purchase friction, the line that failed the stage, gives me nothing to act on.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and the screen admits nobody was asked why on Purchase friction. But Buyer and payer says 'the 2 who said no' and shows one quote, and Joanna's quote reads as her MD agreeing quickly, which is not a no.
screens.why_b6: Andreas's arithmetic was new to me: at 4% missed calls across nine hotels, €1,000 a hotel a month costs more than the bookings recover. So were Ingrid's after-hours call center and Karim's ask for proof on his own numbers, none of which I wrote.
screens.instead: Say plainly that the failed Purchase friction line has no reasons because the four who expect a longer review were never asked why, and that the price objections are about proof on their own numbers and per-hotel cost at low miss rates, so lead with a free measured month and price on recovered bookings.

screens.why1: On a link sent to me as the person who chooses and pays for booking tools, opening with the idea under 'The buying decision' makes clear why it is there, before anything is asked about buying it.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are my everyday words, but the opening line 'Codyco, a confirmed booking in the PMS' calls the product a booking, so I only grasp what it is when I reach the second paragraph.
screens.why3: Unanswered calls after hours and at peak are exactly what I deal with in our reservations office, so I can picture this in my own hotels.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options shown.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks that shouldn't, but the first line names an outcome instead of saying it is an AI that answers booking calls, and the belief only repeats 'answer the calls nobody picks up' rather than turning those calls into bookings.
screens.why6: Most of it says well in short sentences, but 'Imagine Codyco, a confirmed booking in the PMS' sounds odd heard once, and the three system names in a row are a small mouthful.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI that answers your hotels' unanswered booking calls. [same how lines] The people building it believe it would turn the calls nobody picks up into confirmed bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the idea, asking how many of our reservation calls slipped away last month is the obvious first question about what the problem costs us.
screens.why2: 'Lost' is vague to me: I'd ask whether it means abandoned or unanswered calls, which I track as an abandon rate, or calls that were answered but didn't book.
screens.why3: Our CRO reports give me the abandon rate every month, so I'd answer around 6% without guessing.
screens.why4: A percent box suits this, but the 'None' chip repeats typing 0 and leaves two escape chips where one would do.
screens.why5: The founder's 'not every one gets answered' became 'lost', which also covers calls answered but not converted, so the meaning has drifted a little.
screens.why6: The question says well, but 'a percent of the reservation calls last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a mouthful to hear once.
screens.instead: Last month, about what share of reservation calls to your central office went unanswered or were abandoned? A percent, or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after the idea and the question about lost calls, asking what it would be worth to me per hotel is the natural next step for the person who signs for booking tools.
screens.why2: Up front, a month and per hotel are how I already compare channel managers and call-center tools, and the euro bands read cleanly.
screens.why3: I budget setup and monthly fees per property for our tools, so I can place this against what we pay today.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and the range is realistic, but many tools I buy have no setup fee, so 'Under €1,000' has to stand in for 'nothing up front, just the monthly'.
screens.why5: The card says Codyco is 'a confirmed booking in the PMS', which is the outcome rather than the thing, so I price something I can only half picture, perhaps an answering service.
screens.why6: The four options and the two-step bands hold well by ear, but 'Or say you can't say' trips when spoken.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, a tool that answers missed booking calls and puts a confirmed booking in your PMS. What would it be worth to you up front, per hotel? Nothing up front; Under €1,000; €1,000 to under €3,000; €3,000 or more; or I wouldn't pay for this. Or say: I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, asking where the money would actually come from is the obvious next thing for someone who signs off on reservation tools.
screens.why2: I'd answer at once, but the question is about a future purchase and the options slip into the past ('we already had', 'there was no budget'), so I have to read it twice.
screens.why3: Whether this would come from the central reservations budget, a new line, or another cost centre is exactly what I know and decide.
screens.why4: 'There was no budget for it' is not a source of money and is in the wrong tense, and the answer most of us in a hotel group would give, charged back to each hotel's own budget, isn't there.
screens.why5: The read-back drops the 'per hotel' I priced on and states a monthly figure as if I'd said both in one breath, so it drifts a little from what I gave.
screens.why6: Short and one question with four holdable options, but 'Or say you can't say' trips aloud and the past-tense options jar against 'if you went ahead'.
screens.instead: If you went ahead at that price per hotel, where would the money come from? A budget we already have · A new budget someone signs off · Charged to each hotel's own budget · Taken from other spending · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after I said where the money would come from, asking whether I can approve the spend myself is the obvious next step in the buying decision.
screens.why2: Signing off on a per-hotel amount is everyday language for me, and I understand it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know my own approval limit and who else has to approve a tool purchase at our group, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The group's own management, our Geschäftsführer or CFO, is the usual approver for me and has no option of its own; it gets lumped into 'someone else's decision', which overlaps with 'the hotel's owner', and 'Yes' sits oddly second among the 'No's.
screens.why5: I said €3,000 to €5,000 up front plus €1,000 to €2,500 a month, so 'about €3,000' takes only the bottom of my range and drops the monthly cost I would also have to get approved.
screens.why6: The stem is short and the four options are easy to hold, but hearing a 'yes' buried between three 'no's makes the list harder to follow, and 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about €3,000 per hotel, plus the monthly fee, yourself, or would someone else have to agree? Yes, I could sign off myself · No, our managing director or CFO would · No, the hotel's owner would · No, several people would have to agree · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I can sign off myself, the next real hurdle for any tool that touches guest calls in Germany is the DSGVO review, so it is obvious why it is asked here.
screens.why2: Data protection review is everyday language for me; every new CRS or call tool goes past our Datenschutzbeauftragter, and the question reads clearly on first pass.
screens.why3: I have taken booking and telephony tools through our data protection checks before, so I can say from experience roughly how long one like this would take.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover the realistic range for us, 'It wouldn't be needed' is a fair if unlikely answer, and 'I can't tell' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It asks about one concrete step in buying the tool named on the idea card, in words I would use, and nothing else about the founder's plans comes through.
screens.why6: One short question, four options I can hold, the escape said last, then a simple either-or for the band, which is easy to answer by ear.

screens.why1: I just said the data protection review of guest calls would take months, so being asked what would slow it down follows naturally.
screens.why2: Short and plain; I can answer it straight away with our data protection officer, the works council and IT security.
screens.why3: I have bought booking and telephony tools before and know exactly who has to sign off and where it stalls.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's question about what slows the purchase and leaks nothing beyond the product name I was already shown.
screens.why6: One short question, easy to hear once and answer in a sentence or two.

screens.why1: After the price, the budget, the sign-off and the data protection review, asking whether I would actually put €3,000 on a pilot is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: A paid pilot at one hotel with the money back if it does not work is plain to me as a revenue director, and the PMS on the card is my own trade's word.
screens.why3: I decide on and pay for tools like this for our hotels, so I can answer this from my own budget and judgement.
screens.why4: The options lean one way: there is 'Probably not' but no 'Probably yes', so a cautious yes has nowhere to go except the full yes.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's €3,000 per hotel and the money-back pilot, and nothing leaks beyond the idea card I was already shown.
screens.why6: It is easy to follow when heard, but the first option repeats the whole stem and is a mouthful next to the short 'probably not; or no'.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel, or not? Yes · Probably yes · Probably not · No
